articles.title: Senate Republicans return to Capitol furious with Trump after big losses
articles.summary: Senate Republicans returning to the Capitol on Monday are furious with President Trump, whom they blame for last week’s big losses in Senate and House races....
articles.body:
Senate Republicans returning to the Capitol on Monday are furious with President Trump, whom they blame for last week's big losses in Senate and House races.

The anger is raising the chances that the party could pivot away from the lame-duck president in the lead-up to the 2028 presidential election, according to GOP aides and strategists.

Tensions are also rising with Trump's Friday announcement that immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller will be his new chief of staff, replacing the outgoing Susie Wiles.

The Miller appointment suggests a doubling down on the president's policies, particularly on immigration enforcement, after an election in which Hispanic voters swung decisively toward Democrats, especially in Texas.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) on Sunday said Miller should be fired, not promoted.

"If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people," Stutzman said in an interview on CNN. "You don't promote those who are — who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered."

Whit Ayres, a prominent Republican pollster, said Senate Republicans will be less deferential to Trump after suffering a huge loss of seats in last week's election.

Ayres said Trump "clearly will remain the leader of the party for the next two years, but I also think the knee-jerk obeisance to whatever his whims are at the moment is likely over."

"There is so much resentment particularly among Republicans in the Senate for what Donald Trump did in North Carolina and South Carolina and Texas," he said, referring to Trump's endorsement of candidates Michael Whatley, Darline Graham and Ken Paxton, who all lost by large margins in the general election.

"I think his iron grip over the Senate Republicans is likely to be loosened," Ayres said.

One senior Senate Republican aide predicted GOP senators and the broader party will begin to shift away from Trump over the next year.

"Trump said he was on the ballot. He wasn't on the ballot but acted like he was on the ballot," and "a lot of people" voted as if Trump was atop the GOP ticket when they voted for Democrats in battleground states around the country, the aide said.

"We need somebody who can work together with people, who doesn't just try to divide — who is focused on real issues that people care about that are of importance versus stupid little internet memes, which it seems like Trump and Vance are more focused on now," the aide argued.

Republican sources say Trump undermined their chances of winning key Senate races by endorsing weak candidates, such as Paxton and Graham, and by failing to adhere to any message discipline.

GOP senators are also frustrated by what they saw as Trump's reluctance to spend from his massive campaign war chest until late in the campaign.

Senate Republican aides and pollsters say Trump's dismal influence on races across the country will spark an intense discussion about what's next for the party and whether it's time to turn the page on MAGA and its policies.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and members of his leadership team lobbied Trump for months to back Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) over Paxton, the state attorney general, in the Texas Senate Republican primary — or to at least stay neutral — but Trump ignored their advice and endorsed Paxton before the primary runoff, sinking Cornyn's chances.

Thune and his leadership team urged the president and Senate GOP colleagues to keep their political messaging focused on their legislative accomplishments, especially the popular tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, such as its tax deductions for tips.

But Trump instead often veered off from the plan, getting into fights over the White House ballroom, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the Kennedy Center, the East Potomac Park golf course and other topics that GOP strategists viewed as unhelpful to delivering the broader Republican message.

Trump blamed last week's losses on poor Republican candidates, but many Senate Republicans think the blame for the loss of at least seven seats lies squarely with the unpopular president.

"We're up here talking about the generational benefits of avoiding a $4 trillion-plus tax hike and everything else that's inside that bill, and then the president is talking about the Reflecting Pool or the ballroom, and those are the things that get the headlines," a Senate GOP aide said. "Message synchronization was off."

Senate Republicans were galled when Trump dismissed the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act as a "big yawn."

GOP leaders were touting the bipartisan legislation as a major accomplishment to address housing affordability, but Trump popped their balloon as he said he cared more about passing the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a package to overhaul election rules that had virtually no chance of passing Congress.

Senate Republican sources also said Trump waited too long to spend the hundreds of millions of dollars he stockpiled ahead of the midterm elections.

"They sat on that $400 million until it was too late to start spending it," a second GOP aide said.

Trump said in August he would spend "a lot" of money from a pro-Trump super PAC to help "good" GOP candidates, but Senate GOP strategists complained the president's political allies waited until the final weeks of the campaign to dump money into races, which diluted their firepower because they had to pay higher television ad rates.

Trump announced in late October that he would end up spending more than $400 million by Election Day to help Republicans keep Congress.

When Republicans got blown out on Election Day, the White House blamed GOP candidates for not putting in as much effort as the president to promote their candidacies and records.

Trump declared on election night: "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

Senate Republicans say they think Trump also hurt them by constantly bashing their failure to pass the SAVE America Act, even after Republicans held at least five votes on the legislation, either in whole or in part, and came nowhere close to collecting the 60 votes the bill needed to advance.

Trump warned Senate Republicans would be "in big trouble" if they didn't abolish the filibuster to ram the bill through the chamber.

"When you're casting your own teammate as the opponent, what message does that send to the voter?" the GOP aide said.

A third Senate Republican aide argued that Trump clearly deserves the blame for the loss of seven — and maybe as many as nine — Senate seats and more than 40 House seats.

"Trump's message was, 'I'm going to deliver you a good economy,' and it seems like the only person who benefited from the economy was him," the aide said, adding that Democrats successfully tied together voters' concerns about rising prices and corruption in Washington.

"Those two things led to a disaster with independents," the aide said.

The GOP aide said some Senate Republicans expect more "pushback to Trump because his half-life is rapidly diminishing" but cautioned that "he's still a popular figure in the Republican Party."

The president's elevation of Miller, who is seen as a conservative hard-liner, may be a bid to keep base MAGA voters firmly in his corner.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), one of Miller's sharpest critics in the Senate GOP conference, called his elevation to chief of staff a "colossal mistake."

"The worst of all possible choices," Tillis told CNN's Jake Tapper. "The president needs to rethink it."

Senate Republican candidate John Sununu blamed Trump for his double-digit loss to Rep. Chris Pappas (D) in New Hampshire, a state that Senate GOP leaders in August saw as a promising opportunity to flip a Democratic-held seat.

Sununu said Trump's failure to end the months-long conflict with Iran and a steady stream of media stories about Trump's family business dealings sunk his chances of winning.

"This president ran and won on a platform of no more needless, endless wars. And then he attacked Iran, and we're still in it," he told SiriusXM's "The John Kasich Show."

"This president ran on and won on a platform of drain the swamp, right? … And now it seems like he or his family is in on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington," he said. "And those two things, I think, caused people to say, 'You know, I just can't vote for a Republican while he's still in office.'"

Cornyn argued Trump "misread his mandate" after the 2024 election.

He argued the president's "arbitrary" decisions on tariffs raised prices for millions of Americans without improving trade deals, and the administration's "hyperaggressive" immigration enforcement efforts went well beyond what voters expected.

"Voters wanted to retool our trading relationships, but got arbitrary 'Liberation Day' tariffs that raised prices without creating incentives for long-term reshoring. Voters wanted secure borders and peaceful streets, but got hyperaggressive immigration enforcement," Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed.

Other Republicans have stepped up to defend Thune and Senate GOP leaders, arguing that they had little control over the negative political environment that Trump played a major role in creating.

"I don't think any rational, honest person … could blame John Thune for any of this," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) told reporters shortly before the election. "I don't think anybody could blame him for any bad outcome."

Asked if Trump would get most of the blame if Republicans lost control of the Senate, Cramer only said, "There will be a lot of finger-pointing."

articles.title: The Wild Turnover of the Midterms Shows That Living Life Requires Ignoring Government
articles.summary: As the major parties cycle in and out of power, freedom requires defying intrusive laws.
articles.body:
There are lessons to take from last week's blue tidal wave which swept Republicans from power in Congress and across much of the country, just as there were from the 2024 ejection of Democrats from office. Among other things, party turnover underlines the futility of relying on government to maintain predictable conditions and to protect cherished liberties. The midterm elections may have been primarily a rejection of corruption and ineptitude among GOP officials, but they also empowered Democrats to enact an agenda in many places wildly at odds with what prevailed before.

Americans who dread the loss of school choice, violations of gun rights, and increased regulation—or who two years ago feared attacks on reproductive liberty and immigrants—must accept that much of the future of freedom requires defying and undermining intrusive government, no matter who holds office.

Wild Swings in Political Power Don't Indicate Support for Crazy Agendas

Last week's elections removed Republicans from office across the country, much as Democrats were crushed in 2024. Notably, Texas—recently a refuge for those fleeing Democratic dominance in California—flipped largely blue. "For the first time in more than three decades, Democrats have broken Republicans' grip on statewide elections in Texas," observed David Martin Davies of Texas Public Radio. Political refugees must wonder whether the conditions that drove them to move will follow them.

It's true that elections have consequences. But majorities have no more right to impose authoritarian visions than do solo tyrants. And it's not clear that voters booting one party from office are eager to embrace what the other major party has to offer.

Last week, the Associated Press asked voters why they cast their ballots as they did. It found "the cost of living and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans' minds as they cast a ballot in Tuesday's midterm elections." In addition, "the survey also found that while Democrats have at least a slight advantage on several major issues, including the economy and government corruption, the Democratic Party is not much more popular among U.S. voters than the Republican Party."

Americans are hate-voting in election after election. While the shrinking ranks of hardcore partisans still like their parties, Pew Research's Steven Shepard reported last month that majorities of independents who just favor one party "say a major reason they lean toward their preferred party is that the other party's policies are harmful." But "relatively few Republican leaners (34%) and Democratic leaners (27%) say a major reason they lean toward their preferred party is the perceived good of its policies."

The Major Parties Are Taking Turns Alienating Voters

Even so, in our seemingly immutable two-party system, rejecting one of the political tribes means handing the reins of power to the other. Politicians aren't very good at accepting that they're regarded as slightly less awful than the alternative and acting accordingly. They always take the ball and run.

"Democrats will use their new trifecta status in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin to dismantle union reforms, progress on taxes, school choice and litigation reform," cautions The Wall Street Journal 's Kimberley Strassel.

Sure enough, Democratic governors in Arizona and Texas immediately renewed vows to roll back overwhelmingly popular school choice programs, just as their colleagues in Virginia earlier attacked that state's once robust protections for self-defense rights once they gained power.

Voters will have an opportunity in 2028 to reconsider their choices. After all, federal Republicans were spanked this year after they replaced Democrats who sent government spending and resulting inflation soaring, only to implement tariffs and a war that kept prices rising, along with unpopular immigration enforcement . But the wild political swings of recent years suggest the result will be dramatic changes in law and unstable policy environments, with more of the same to follow in the next round of elections.

Americans Tend To Do What They Please, No Matter Politicians' Desires

That doesn't mean we should stop voting for candidates we find less bad than the alternatives; none of us want to live under intolerable governments. But to live our lives through cycles of severe policy changes, engaging in activities that are forbidden under one party and encouraged under the other, we should emulate those Americans of the past who largely ignored government dictates.

Prohibition was famously defeated by noncompliance. "There were twice as many speakeasies in Rochester, New York, as saloons closed by Prohibition. That was more or less true throughout the country," the Cato Institute's Mark Thornton noted in a 1991 analysis .

Likewise for laws against same-sex relationships. "As far back as the 1890s, there were establishments in the Village catering to lesbians and gays," Bedford + Bowery reports , although same-sex conduct wasn't fully legalized in New York until 1980 . The modern gay rights movement kicked off after a fiercely resisted 1969 police raid on the Stonewall bar.

Gambling has long been targeted by law, though restrictions loosened in recent years. While many people who dislike games of chance want bans reimposed, "the result of an attempted ban, as we have seen, is that gamblers go underground," the Competitive Enterprise Institute warned in 2014.

And modern gun control laws have repeatedly met defiance , including "a compliance rate of about 4 percent" with New York's mandatory registration for so-called assault weapons as described by Hudson Valley One . The modern DIY movement to encourage people to manufacture their own firearms is specifically intended to make such laws unenforceable.

Ignoring the law isn't a completely satisfactory replacement for living under a predictable and permissive regime. There's always the risk of arrest. People have little recourse when they get ripped off or otherwise mistreated when engaged in illegal activity. And underground markets empower organized criminals, who are not the safest people to deal with.

But defying laws also helps compel political change. It forces politicians to choose between looking impotent as laws go ignored, or as if they're responsive to popular opinion. Over the years, officeholders who agreed to legalize booze, marijuana, same-sex relationships, concealed carry, and the like weren't always true believers in the cause. But they recognized unbeatable popular resistance when they saw it.

In the years to come, political power will probably continue cycling between two major parties who do their best to overreach and offend the American public. Homeschoolers, reproductive rights advocates, gun owners, and anybody else who votes in hopes of being left alone should consider the lessons of the past. The tenure of dominant parties turns rancid at a seemingly accelerating pace, but living your life as you please without regard for politicians' whims has timeless appeal.

articles.title: Trump: ‘A lot of people didn’t like’ Vance comments blaming midterm losses on Iran war
articles.summary: President Trump said “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President Vance blaming the GOP’s election losses on the Iran war, which has proven to be unpopular a...
articles.body:
President Trump said "a lot of people didn't like" Vice President Vance blaming the GOP's election losses on the Iran war , which has proven to be unpopular across the country.

When asked if Vance's statement following the results of last week's midterms had impacted their relationship, Trump told reporters, "No, not at all."

"But a lot of people didn't like his comments. But not me," he added.

"He was right, other than one thing. He should have made one other statement. One statement that I think is very important. If you had it to do again? Would you do it again? The answer is yes," the president continued. "I can tell you, if I had it to do again, this historically, for history, will go down as one of the best things we ever did."

Vance released a lengthy social media post that detailed why he believed the GOP lost in key battleground elections this cycle.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," he wrote. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."

The vice president was referring to Trump partially blaming the Middle East conflict for Republicans falling short last week. Vance received pushback from both sides of the aisle for the comment.

The president told The Wall Street Journal late Tuesday that the war with Iran, now in its eighth month, "was a piece of it" in an election night interview.

Asked during an interview on CBS's "60 Minutes" about Vance's post and whether he knew it was coming, Trump said: "He asked me, 'What do I think?' I said, 'Write what you feel.'"

He also defended the war effort in the recent interview, saying he believed "historically this will be a very good decision" because "you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."

"Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not, but you know, I have to go with what's right for our country," he added. "If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what happened. I've stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. That's a big thing."

Trump left the door open to renewing military action against Iran but said it was unlikely if peace talks progressed.

articles.title: Which Republicans are running for minority leadership roles in US Congress?
articles.summary: Republicans in US House and Senate will hold elections on Tuesday to select leadership after losing their majorities.
articles.body:
The United States midterm elections have reshaped the balance of power in Washington, DC, breaking the Republican Party’s grip on Congress.

With Democrats set to take control of both legislative chambers in January, Republicans are preparing for a change in congressional leadership.

On Tuesday, Republicans in the House of Representatives and the Senate will hold elections to select the party’s leaders through the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

Several senior positions are at stake, including minority leader, minority whip and conference chair. But what do these jobs entail, and who is competing for them?

What are the key minority leadership positions?

Because the US has long had a two-party system – revolving around Democrats and Republicans – each side organises its own leadership in the chambers of Congress.

The aim is to present a united front on legislation and other congressional matters.

When the 120th Congress is sworn in this January, the Republican Party will be in the minority in both chambers.

Democrats will have majorities of at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate and at least 254 in the House, which has a total of 435 voting members.

To organise as the minority party, Republicans will need to choose leaders for both the House and Senate.

The minority leader in a given chamber is the most senior member of whichever party holds the fewest seats. The leader serves as the party’s chief spokesperson, coordinates its legislative strategy and negotiates with the majority party.

The minority whip is the second-ranking leadership position. The whip counts votes, communicates with lawmakers and works to keep members united behind the party’s positions.

Republicans also elect other leadership positions, including the conference chair, who oversees internal party meetings and helps shape the party’s messaging. Committee chairs also need to be selected to help develop legislative priorities.

Who is running for House minority leadership?

The biggest contest in the House is for minority leader, with longtime rivals Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jim Jordan of Ohio competing for the position.

Scalise, who has held senior Republican leadership positions for more than a decade, served as House majority whip from 2014 to 2018 and minority whip from 2019 to 2022. He has put himself forward as an experienced leader who can unite the party and guide Republicans through their return to the minority.

Jordan, a founding member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus and a close Trump ally, is campaigning on a more aggressive approach to confronting the Democratic majority.

In a letter to colleagues, the Ohio lawmaker described himself as “battle-tested” and argued he could better coordinate the party’s response to Democrat-led investigations into the Trump administration.

The contest for minority whip, the party’s second-ranking position, is between current majority whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota and August Pfluger of Texas.

Emmer is seeking to retain the position. He has acknowledged the scale of the party’s midterm losses, but argued that Republicans must remain united as they move into the minority.

Pfluger, who chairs the Republican Study Committee, is making the case for a change in leadership. In a letter to colleagues, he said the party needed “fresh ideas” and a clearer strategy to win back the House in 2028.

Senate majority leader John Thune of South Dakota is seeking to retain his position as his party’s leader in the chamber.

That would make him the minority leader when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Thune, who succeeded longtime Republican Senate leader Mitch McConnell in 2025, has so far faced no public challenger for the seat.

Republican John Barrasso of Wyoming, currently the majority whip, is also expected to seek another term as the party’s second-ranking leader in the Senate.

There has been some pushback against holding the Senate leadership elections so soon after the midterm losses, though.

Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin has pushed to delay the vote, arguing Republicans should have more time to assess the election results.

“It’s not like we’ve got to quick-form a majority in the Senate and do all the things with the committees. We have time,” Johnson told Fox News.

“This is time for reflection. This is time not to just, quick, make a knee-jerk decision.”

Senators like Mike Lee of Utah have voiced support for Johnson’s campaign.

“We have no business holding Senate Republican leadership elections until: (1) we’ve had ample opportunity to discuss what happened on Tuesday, and (2) we know who’s going to be in our conference,” Lee wrote on social media.

Mike Johnson will lose his position as House speaker when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. The speaker is elected by the entire House, and the majority traditionally nominates someone from within its party.

Johnson announced he will not seek the House minority leader position, clearing the way for Scalise and Jordan to compete for the top Republican post.

However, Johnson is not leaving Congress. He will remain a member of the House and continue representing his Louisiana district.

Tuesday’s internal party elections will determine who leads the Republicans through their transition to minority status as they prepare to challenge Democratic control of Congress.

The leadership race will also test whether Republicans intend to continue backing Trump’s agenda or rethink their approach.

articles.title: Trump says ‘great dislike’ for Israel contributed to Republican midterm losses
articles.summary: The president’s comments underscore a sea change in US politics where Israel once had bipartisan support.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said a "great dislike" for Israel was one of the reasons the Republicans lost in the midterm elections, along with the Iran war and the subsequent rise in gasoline prices.

"I think if I was on the ballot, it would've been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love," Trump said in an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" that aired Sunday . "But there's something beyond that. They didn't like the war. They didn't like the fact that gasoline went up, 'cause I had it down at a low, and there's a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel."

Trump's comments underscore a sea change in US politics where Israel once had bipartisan support, as well as strong backing from Republican and Democratic presidents. But the extent of US military and financial support for Israel emerged as a frequent political liability during the midterm elections.

Michigan's Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed may have been the most prominent critic of Israel during the elections, but he was far from the only one. Even Vice President JD Vance suggested Republicans would have to rethink their once-stalwart support of Israel moving forward.

Trump said he agrees with Vance's position that the war with Iran is among the reasons for the Republican loss. But he said he doesn't regret his decision to launch the war. "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not. But you know, I have to go with what's right for our country. If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened."

The president also said that other countries, including Israel, would have to share the costs of the war.

"Those countries that we've protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we've had for the war 'cause without us, they wouldn't exist. Without us, Israel would not exist," Trump said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long presented himself as the leader best able to manage the relationship with the United States and particularly Trump. But in just a matter of days, Trump has signaled major changes may be coming.

"Democrats and Republicans are competing to see who can distance themselves from us more," wrote Israeli journalist Amir Tibon on X. "And if we don't act quickly, the new Congress will start holding up arms sales." Tibon called for a new government that can begin "repairing the damage Netanyahu is leaving behind."

On the day of the US elections, Trump said he would end $4 billion in annual aid to Israel this year, potentially cutting off one of the key elements of Israel's security strategy. Days later, Netanyahu said the aid would shift to a "partnership," but didn't say whether Trump had given him a heads-up about the surprise announcement.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog made an oblique reference to the shift in American and international perceptions of the country on Sunday, as he tasked Netanyahu's rival, Gadi Eizenkot, with forming the next government.

"The challenges facing the State of Israel are immense. Some demand urgent and immediate attention," he said. "Iran does not pause for a moment in its schemes and threats. We must work to build a diplomatic horizon in the region and for the day after the war."

articles.title: Biden says Trump’s Jan. 6 actions ‘should follow him to his grave’
articles.summary: Former President Joe Biden issued scathing criticism of President Donald Trump in his forthcoming memoir, saying his actions during the Jan.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden issued scathing criticism of President Donald Trump in his forthcoming memoir, saying his actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol “should follow him to his grave.” Biden’s comments, published as a book excerpt in The Atlantic on Monday, mark some of his strongest criticism of Trump since the former president left office. In the excerpt, Biden says Trump “led an insurrection” and slammed his decision to issue sweeping pardons of Jan. 6 defendants. “The criminals who attacked law-enforcement officers that day didn’t deserve pardons,” Biden wrote. “They deserved prison terms.” The former president added that Trump and the president’s supporters “continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement.” “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement,” he wrote. “What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.” Reached for comment, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis called Biden “the worst president in American history.” She pointed to his handling of the border, crime and inflation, adding, “What they did to this country should never be forgotten.” The memoir, “Promise Me, America,” is set to be published on Nov. 17. In a September interview with Time magazine, Trump acknowledged that he was considering pardoning members of his administration before his term concluded, pointing to Biden’s decision to issue preemptive pardons. Biden issued those pardons to his son, Hunter Biden, and other members of his family, lawmakers on the congressional Jan. 6 committee, Dr. Anthony Fauci, and former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Mark Milley. Biden also described his meeting with Trump after the 2024 election, part of a tradition where the outgoing president briefs the incoming president. Biden said that Trump’s tone “bordered on fawning” and said that Trump told him that “if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends” — a remark that the former president said left him “too stunned to respond.” “He said my performance on job creation had been ‘extraordinary,’” Biden wrote. “He added that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me. I didn’t really understand why he was buttering me up, so I cut off his compliments to move on to the business at hand.” During the approximately two hour meeting, Biden said that he wanted to give Trump an overview of world issues that he believed would “dominate his presidency.” “He nodded appreciatively,” Biden said of Trump. “But I noticed a curious pattern: He focused on the personalities of the leaders, as if we were sharing gossip about people at a dinner party, not discussing issues of global significance.” Biden announced Sunday that he would not “be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped,” pointing to his fight against cancer. “Some days are better than others,” Biden said in the post to X. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”

articles.title: Bernie Sanders Wants To Use Democrats' Midterm Victory To Expand Medicare. Has He Looked at Europe?
articles.summary: Sanders wants to expand government-funded health care, even as European countries struggle with rising costs, lengthy waiting lists, and shortages.
articles.body:
Fresh off the Democrats' midterm victory, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I–Vt.) has a lengthy wish list for the incoming Congress, starting with increasing the government's role in healthcare.

"As an immediate first step, Democrats must lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 down to 55, expand Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing, and guarantee universal health care coverage for every child from birth through age 19," Sanders said in a video posted to social media on Thursday. "All of this can be accomplished with 51 votes in the Senate through the reconciliation process."

"Healthcare must be considered as a human right, not a privilege. That means passing Medicare for All legislation, now supported by 66 percent of the American people," he continued.

It may seem easy to simply declare something a human right and decide that everyone must have universal access. But we do not need to look at imagined models created by academics to know what Sanders' dream of "Medicare for All" would look like. We need only to look across the pond.

The United Kingdom has a National Health Service (NHS), which is entirely "free" at the point of use. Despite its record levels of spending, Britain's waiting list for hospital treatment rose to 7.4 million people in August (the most recent month for which data are available) and the 18-week treatment target has not been met in more than a decade. For emergency care, almost 40 percent of patients wait longer than 4 hours. (Americans spend an average of 2.5 hours in the emergency room, Axios reported in April.)

These waits have deadly consequences. As Hyphen reports , 79,130 names were taken off the waiting list from September 2024 through August 2025—not because they were treated, but because they died before getting to the front of the queue. Just last month, a 59-year-old delivery driver died of a heart attack while waiting for surgery.

The NHS performs poorly on almost every available measure. Survival rates for the most common types of cancer rank near the bottom of European countries, and the U.K. has one of the lowest five-year survival rates for breast, cervical, colorectal, and lung cancers compared to high-income countries.

Although Britain has one of the most socialized healthcare systems in Europe, other countries also face the same supply issues. France spends 11.4 percent of GDP on healthcare—well above average for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)—and yet 4.1 percent of people in France reported unmet healthcare needs, compared with an OECD average of 3.4 percent. Just 60 percent were satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare, below the OECD average of 64 percent (and considerably lower than the 75 percent reported in the United States).

Americans also face far lower waiting times. According to the OECD , 42 percent of Americans waited at least a month for a specialist appointment in 2023, compared to 62 percent in Britain and 65 percent in France.

These systems not only offer poor quality care; they cost taxpayers an enormous amount of money, straining public finances. Much of the world is suffering from a demographic crisis, in which there are more elderly people (who require more healthcare) than younger, working people. But these problems are exacerbated in European countries because of their enormous welfare states.

The recent violent protests in France—in which a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off, historic buildings were set on fire, and a head teacher was doused in gasoline—are an extreme, though not unrealistic, example of what can happen when politicians make promises to spend more money the government does not have. European countries are saddled with debt , and yet the populace demands more.

America's healthcare system is far from perfect. Sanders is right to call it "dysfunctional" and "wildly expensive." But his plan to give the government—which, through Medicare, Medicaid, and other programs, is already responsible for 48 percent of U.S. healthcare spending—is misguided. The government is heavily involved here from a regulatory perspective too, including deciding what treatments are allowed, what drugs can be marketed, and what insurance plans must cover.

And Europe is no model for reform. If anything, it show how bad things can get when government has even more control over the healthcare system.

articles.title: Josh Shapiro says Texas won’t replace Pennsylvania as the ‘ultimate swing state’
articles.summary: The governor romped to a 22-point reelection victory last week.
articles.body:
Democrats' blue wave blew up the 2028 battle map. But Josh Shapiro insists Texas isn't going to replace Pennsylvania as the "ultimate swing state."

Shapiro's theory of the case for 2028 has long rested on his ability to win resoundingly and repeatedly in what has recently been the nation's biggest battleground state. On Tuesday, he helped deliver Democrats four congressional flips and their first trifecta in Harrisburg in three decades, all while running up a more than 20-point margin in his own reelection bid. He plowed over $10 million into state Democrats' campaign arms and helped recruit and cut ads for candidates across House and state Senate races. He also flipped 11 counties President Donald Trump won in 2024 and, his team argued in a post-election memo shared first with POLITICO, showed "unique strength" with voters skeptical of the Democratic Party.

It's a significant show of force even in a wave election — one that could springboard him into a presidential bid if he chooses, even as Democrats turn their attention to redder turf .

"The common-sense approach we've taken to governing, the kind of candidates we recruited to run for Congress who won, I think that that can be a model for our party," Shapiro told POLITICO by phone late last week. And "it's going to be important that we share our Pennsylvania model from what I would maintain … is still the ultimate swing state."

Shapiro continues to play coy about his presidential ambitions . He phoned Democrats' primary kingmaker, Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) , after the election, but declined to discuss the details. When POLITICO asked Shapiro his timeline to decide a 2028 run, he replied: "I just wrapped up a meeting with the legislative leaders and my senior team to work on our agenda going forward, and that's what I'm focused on right now."

Here's more from POLITICO's chat with Shapiro, edited and condensed for length.

You've got your trifecta. What's your No. 1 priority?

The first bill that will reach my desk will be to raise the minimum wage to 15 bucks an hour. I've been able to get a lot of stuff done through the Republican Legislature, but that's an example of something that hasn't.

Is signing onto the National Popular Vote Compact something you'd be interested in?

I have said that I am open to that, I think I've voiced some positivity toward it. As it relates to the trifecta, though, the leaders and I agreed that we would speak with one voice in announcing our initial agenda.

A lot of Democrats are saying the biggest message that they got out of this wave election was the economy. Do you think that that's the biggest takeaway?

I think in part that is correct, and that's why the first new law I want to pass in Pennsylvania is to put more money in people's pockets. I also think there was something deeper. … Substantively the issue that obviously mattered most was the high cost of everything; I think underneath that was a real fear that people had about the direction this country was going in, and they wanted to use their power to change it.

Do you think the path to the presidency is moving out of the Blue Wall and into states like Texas, into the Sun Belt?

Democrats are proving that we can win everywhere. … We added back to the Blue Wall. Ohio, with Amy [Acton]'s incredible victory there. I was proud to campaign for her.

We're showing we can win in these southern states. So I think the takeaway from Tuesday night is the map got a whole lot bigger for Democrats. And so long as Republicans continue to follow Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance off the cliff, their map is getting much smaller.

Do you think that Texas will take over from Pennsylvania as the nation's biggest swing state?

I mean, they're a big state, and they were just won by two outstanding Democrats. I was so impressed with both of them and how they ran their campaigns. And I imagine Texas is going to have a lot to say about the future leadership in our country.

But not necessarily taking over Pennsylvania's spot

I mean, come on. I'm Pennsylvania first. You're never going to get me to come off of Pennsylvania being the ultimate swing state.

Abdul El-Sayed told me he hopes the next Democratic presidential nominee shares his views on Israel. He opposes military aid to Israel. Do you agree that that's the stance the nominee, whoever it is, should take?

Well, he is one voice in our party. And I look forward to getting a chance to talk to him and learn more about how he really thinks and how he really views these issues, and having a thoughtful conversation with him.

Is there anyone coming out of Tuesday who you want to talk to, who you think 'that person has a good message for the party'?

I've talked to probably more than 20 people across the country since Tuesday night who won races at all levels. I've been incredibly impressed by the talent that chose to run for office and won in really tough states. I think I can learn from a lot of them, and I want to learn from them, and I want to listen to them, and I salute their victories.

articles.title: Los Angeles mayoral race points to growing sway of democratic socialists
articles.summary: Nithya Raman taps into frustration with economic and political status quo to become mayor of the second-largest US city.
articles.body:
Los Angeles, United States – On November 5, Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman was declared the winner of the local mayoral race, defeating the incumbent, Karen Bass, with nearly 53 percent of the vote.

“Los Angeles, I am deeply honoured to be your next mayor,” Raman, 45, said in a video shared on social media after the results were announced.

“I love this city. I believe in its people. The work ahead will be hard, and change will take time. And together, we are going to build a future as extraordinary as the city we call home.”

Raman’s victory is the latest example of a candidate who identifies as a democratic socialist notching a win in a major election.

When she takes office in December, Los Angeles will join an expanding list of cities overseen or soon to be led by democratic socialist mayors.

They include New York City; Seattle, Washington; Providence, Rhode Island; and the capital of the United States, Washington, DC.

Those successes have been fueled by a series of factors, including the popular belief that the political and economic status quo favours the wealthy.

“The idea that the economy is rigged is pretty common,” said Shawn Gude, author of the book American Socialist: The Life and Legacy of Eugene V Debs.

The book profiles Debs, a political leader and presidential candidate who helped galvanise a socialist movement in the US in the early 1900s. Gude explained that the struggle for common Americans to access basic services and necessities has long fuelled such movements.

“Democratic socialists have been effective at tapping into that anger and a desire for something better,” he said.

Raman’s victory was one of several results in the 2026 midterm elections that underscored the rise of democratic socialism — and its main organising body, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — as a serious force in US politics.

“DSA has quadrupled our presence in the halls of Congress, sending a socialist bloc to DC that will fight to put people over profits,” the organisation said in a statement following the elections.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a DSA member, was not on the ballot this year, but his focus on cost-of-living issues and affordability was adopted by other Democrats, including three congressional candidates he endorsed.

All three — Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier — won seats in Congress for the first time during this year’s midterms.

In Colorado, a 29-year-old Ethiopian immigrant named Melat Kiros also claimed victory in her congressional race with DSA support after toppling a Democratic incumbent in the party primary.

Los Angeles similarly saw democratic socialists score wins in municipal races and pick up a seat in California’s 34th Congressional District, where Angela Gonzales-Torres defeated Democratic incumbent Jimmy Gomez.

Critics say that establishment candidates often rely on an advantage in funding over socialist rivals.

But Leslie Chang, the cochair of the Los Angeles DSA, says the organisation tries to make up for those disadvantages with an enthusiasm and ground game that their opponents cannot match.

“DSA really leans heavily on our field operations. We bring people into our movement through face-to-face conversations at the doors,” Chang said.

While the number of democratic socialists in elected office remains relatively small in the US, the movement’s victories in recent years represent a remarkable shift.

When Senator Bernie Sanders launched his 2016 presidential run, he became the first major political figure in recent memory to test the viability of democratic socialism at the national level.

But critics dismissed his campaign as out of touch with political reality.

A decade later, even moderate candidates have adopted some of his rhetoric on issues such as corporate power and the corrosive effect of economic inequality on politics.

A YouGov poll released in October found that 50 percent of voters said they would be willing to cast a ballot for a democratic socialist. Other once-fringe left-wing positions, such as ending US support for Israel, have also become increasingly popular.

But that growth has also raised questions within the movement over how much compromise is acceptable to accommodate the demands of electoral politics.

Those questions have sometimes led to fractious internal debates.

A day before the November 3 election, for instance, a national DSA panel held a vote on whether to withdraw Raman’s endorsement over her past positions on Israel, including whether she had adequately supported the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement.

The vote failed by 14 to 13, narrowly avoiding what critics said would be an unforced error just days before the election.

One thread that connects many democratic socialists is a focus on good governance and municipal administration.

Raman certainly fits that mould. She previously worked as an urban planner and promised to bring her passion for policy details to issues such as housing and homelessness. Her campaign slogan promised, “a city that works”.

Chang says DSA’s interest in municipal administration continues beyond election day.

She hopes democratic socialists will stay engaged with constituents on larger issues as well as services like rubbish pick-up and infrastructure fixes.

“In four years, if we’re going to be knocking on doors and asking for these voters to support our candidate again, we don’t want to be in a situation where they say, ‘Well, I voted for you last time, and nothing got better,’” she said.

Gude said this focus was also shared by an earlier generation of socialists, who gained popularity in cities across the country through measures like bringing sewage systems to poor neighbourhoods and building public parks.

“Mamdani talks about pothole politics,” said Gude. “In the Debs era, this was called sewer socialism.”

“On a practical level, it’s about trying to deliver for working people directly and build the movement from the ground up,” he added. “It’s a way of showing people that they can trust you to make tangible improvements in their lives.”

articles.title: NYC ICE chief fires back at far-left politicians seeking to abolish agency: 'Change the law'
articles.summary: Kenneth Genalo challenges lawmakers calling for ICE's abolition, saying they should change immigration law instead of demonizing federal agents.
articles.body: New York City's top immigration enforcement official has a blunt message for far-left politicians demanding the abolition of ICE: Change the law instead of demonizing federal agents who put their lives on the line enforcing it. Kenneth Genalo, who leads ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) in New York City, issued the challenge during an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, taking aim at elected officials who have increasingly called to dismantle the agency. "If you don't like the job we're doing and the priorities and the people that we're targeting, change the law," Genalo said. "Congressional people, senators, representatives. Change the law, don't demonize ICE for doing the job that you empowered us to do." The remarks came during a recent Fox News Digital ride-along with ICE in Brooklyn, where agents arrested two men, including one facing a pending felony sexual abuse charge, and another who had served seven years in prison for assault, according to ICE. INSIDE ICE'S HIGH-STAKES RAIDS TARGETING ILLEGAL MIGRANTS IN NYC AS CHIEF RIPS SANCTUARY LAWS Growing calls to abolish ICE Genalo's rebuke comes amid a widening campaign to abolish ICE and increasingly heated rhetoric directed at federal immigration agents. In July, no less than 143 New York elected officials, including 31 of the city's 51 Council members, signed a letter urging congressional Democrats to dismantle the agency, accusing ICE of widespread abuses and portraying it as a threat to public safety and democracy. The signatories argued that ICE could no longer be reformed and urged congressional Democrats to defund and dismantle it. They also cited the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration enforcement officers in Minneapolis as evidence of what they described as the agency's disregard for public safety. Among the signatories was newly elected New York Democrat Claire Valdez, who has also made abolishing ICE part of her congressional platform. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., have also separately called for dismantling the agency. Genalo blamed inflammatory political rhetoric for emboldening anti-ICE protesters and escalating tensions during enforcement operations. He questioned why activists would interfere with arrests without knowing the criminal histories of those being targeted, pointing to an operation during the Brooklyn ride-along in which protesters disrupted ICE agents attempting to apprehend an Ecuadorian national facing child sexual abuse charges, according to ICE. "Why would you protest that we're trying to arrest this individual?" he asked. WATCH: Inside ICE’s high-stakes NYC street arrests as sanctuary laws complicate operations MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION' For Genalo, the increasingly hostile rhetoric overlooks the people behind the badges — officers enforcing laws enacted by Congress while confronting potentially dangerous suspects and protesters. "We're mothers, we're fathers, we are brothers, we have sisters, sons and daughters, and we're doing our job," he said. The Brooklyn-born, 34-year law enforcement veteran argued that politicians were vilifying agents for carrying out their duties, even as restrictions on local cooperation force ICE to pursue suspects on public streets rather than take them into custody in secure jails. Genalo said such encounters expose officers, suspects and bystanders to dangers that could be avoided through cooperation with local authorities. During the Brooklyn ride-along, Genalo said both men arrested had previously been in local custody but were released despite ICE detainer requests. A warning rooted in 9/11 Genalo's concerns about the breakdown in cooperation drew on his experience responding to one of the darkest days in New York's history. The veteran official recalled being deployed to ground zero after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, warning that New York was forgetting lessons about the importance of cooperation between federal and local law enforcement. "I go back to 9/11, I do it all the time because I was there, I was deployed, SRT, I was down at ground zero," he recalled. He cited the 9/11 Commission's findings about failures in cooperation and intelligence sharing, drawing a parallel to the restrictions ICE faces today. "We should be standing arm-in-arm with our NYPD brethren, helping the city," Genalo said, recalling a time when ICE worked more closely with local authorities. The agency once maintained a dedicated unit at Rikers Island that reviewed the immigration status of foreign-born inmates before their release, Genalo said. Agents took more than 100 people a week into federal custody through the arrangement, which he blamed former Mayor Bill de Blasio for ending. Genalo said former Mayor Eric Adams later tried to restore cooperation, but faced City Council restrictions. New York's escalating ICE showdown The political confrontation with ICE has since intensified under Mamdani. On Nov. 2, Mamdani threatened legal action over ICE's alleged unauthorized use of city-owned parking lots in a letter addressed directly to Genalo and other federal officials. Genalo had criticized the mayor's efforts to discourage private businesses from allowing ICE agents to use their parking facilities during the Fox News Digital interview, four days before the letter was issued. DHS rejected the mayor's position in a statement to Fox News Digital on Saturday. "Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t. Luckily, no terminated parking will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make New York safe again," a DHS spokesperson said. "We need New York to cooperate with our officers and stop RELEASING criminals from their jails into New York’s neighborhoods. Seven of the 10 safest cities in America cooperate with ICE." DHS also provided Fox News Digital with examples of migrants it identified as public safety threats arrested in New York City, including individuals it said had convictions for sexual assault, weapons offenses and robbery. The confrontation with ICE has also extended to the state level. On Nov. 6, Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James reminded local governments of a Nov. 25 deadline to terminate agreements allowing their facilities to hold people solely for federal civil immigration detention under the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act. Genalo criticized the legislation, arguing that it would extend restrictions on ICE cooperation beyond New York City to the rest of the state. He also challenged city leaders to put cooperation with ICE on the ballot and let New Yorkers decide for themselves — a demand that takes on added significance given the 31 City Council members who signed the abolition letter. But Genalo said the City Council had refused to put the question before voters. "The City Council voted no, they didn't want to do that. I wonder why," he said. For Genalo, the growing political opposition reflects what he described as a fundamental misunderstanding of ICE's mission and the officers carrying it out. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He argued that immigration enforcement has continued under successive administrations, but the rhetoric directed at agents has become increasingly hostile, with politicians and the media vilifying officers rather than acknowledging the work they do. "They don't realize the ramifications that their verbiage has," Genalo said. "But instead we're getting demonized by politicians, by congressional people, by mayors, by governors, by the media."

articles.title: Trump questions elections integrity after previously accepting midterm results
articles.summary: Trump made the claims, without evidence, on Truth Social on Monday.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.

Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.

Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.

Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing.

The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

"We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported," he said.

Stewart added that in some states, like Florida and Georgia, some initial reporting of results happens quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots.

Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.

"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.

Surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate.

As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi.

"State laws and practicalities are such that some states will just take longer to count," said Ruth Greenwood, director of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School.

"That doesn't mean anything nefarious is occurring—we just need to trust local election officials to count every vote and tell us the results when they are done."

The outcome has been clear since election night. Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."

He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat.

"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said.

Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.

In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.

He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.

The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.

Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.

Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.

Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.

Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes

Judge dismisses Trump administration's lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans in Alaska election

articles.title: Congress returns for lame-duck sprint after GOP midterm losses
articles.summary: Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill for the first time since the midterm elections, which delivered a slew of Democratic victories that will dramatically...
articles.body:
Washington — Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill on Monday for the first time since the midterm elections, which delivered a slew of Democratic victories that will dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington in the new year.

Now, with the sun setting on their majorities, Republicans are aiming to make the most of their lame-duck period. But first, they'll select their new leaders — and work to prevent a possible government shutdown.

House and Senate Republicans are set to hold their leadership elections on Tuesday, while House Democrats will hold theirs the following week, and Senate Democrats will elect their leaders in early December.

On the House side, Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping aside after the GOP's extensive losses last week , leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, to jockey for minority leader. Rep. August Pfluger is challenging Majority Whip Tom Emmer for the position of minority whip. Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain has two opponents — Reps. Erin Houchin and Greg Steube.

Democrats up for a handful of leadership positions are running unopposed. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become speaker, with House Whip Katherine Clark as majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar as whip. Rep. Joe Neguse is set to become assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu, the current Democratic Caucus vice chair, chair of the Democratic Caucus.

In the upper chamber, Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Tuesday morning. But at least a handful of Senate GOP members, led by Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, want to delay their elections to recalibrate after last week's electoral bloodbath for the party.

In a letter to Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, who chairs the Senate Republican Conference, the Wisconsin Republican argued that "we need to have serious discussions within our conference" about 2028, after the party's "stunning defeat."

"Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice," the senator wrote in the letter seeking to compel a conference meeting before moving forward with the leadership elections.

Johnson said the letter would be signed by at least five of his colleagues, per Senate rules. Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Mike Lee of Utah, Rick Scott of Florida and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania were among those expressing support for the effort.

In an interview with "The Takeout with Major Garrett" on Friday, Johnson said the letter was not "hostile" to Senate Majority Leader John Thune or other leaders. No senator has announced a challenge to Thune, and his conference widely expects him to be elected to a second term as leader. But the Wisconsin Republican argued that there's "no reason to rush," noting that the GOP doesn't yet know the size of its conference with the outcome of two races — Mississippi and Alaska — still unresolved.

"There's a lot of reason for robust discussion and reflection about what went wrong," he said.

As for Senate Democrats, leadership elections are slated for early next month. And with Democrats' overperformance of expectations in the midterms, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has appeared to improve his standing, despite facing intense criticism over the last two years for his leadership that originated with a fight over funding the government.

After Congress approved a stopgap measure to keep the government funded earlier this year, funding is set to run out on Dec. 11, teeing up a familiar fight on Capitol Hill.

Lawmakers now have a condensed timeline to negotiate and pass the 12 annual appropriations bills that fund the federal government, or opt to kick the can down the road further.

The initial deadline to fund the government was Sept. 30, but Congress approved a short-term extension in a move that avoided a messy funding fight ahead of the midterm elections.

In an interview with CBS News in late October, Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said House and Senate negotiators "will start to do business" after the election, acknowledging that Democrats would have more leverage after the midterms if they won the majority.

Asked about the points of agreement and disagreement between Democrats and Republicans, DeLauro said, "we're going to find out when we sit down and talk about it."

"What I am going to work to do is to pass all 12 appropriations bills, if we can," she said. "No one wants a continuing resolution that goes through next year."

"As it unfolds, we will see what we have to do and where we go," she said.

The war in Iran could take center stage in the funding fight, as some Democrats advocate for using their leverage to block funds for the unpopular conflict. But doing so could risk a shutdown that could spill into the new Congress, and detract from other priorities. Congress also faces an end-of-year deadline to pass its annual defense policy bill, which could also be complicated by opposition to the Iran war and Pentagon leadership that's been under scrutiny after the GOP's significant losses.

Anger toward Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which was simmering before the elections, boiled over after the GOP's crippling losses, with intense criticism over his strategy in the Iran war.

GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, a frequent thorn in the side of Republican leadership, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September, but House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.

But since then, the environment has appeared to grow less favorable for Hegseth, and some Republicans, who were once fierce defenders of Hegseth, appear to be reconsidering their support for him.

"I can tell you with a high level of confidence, there's a lot of questions about Hegseth," Rep. James Comer, who leads the House Oversight Committee, said in an interview with News Nation. "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran. I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."

Massie said he plans to push ahead with forcing a vote on Hegseth's impeachment upon Congress' return, unless he resigns.

"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said last week.

A day later, Massie warned that his impeachment resolution "is a much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress."

"They'll have hearings & trials," he posted on social media .

Other Republicans remained noncommittal about whether they would support the impeachment effort, like Rep. French Hill of Arkansas. Hill said he's not satisfied with how the war has been handled, but he drew a distinction between Hegseth's job performance and whether he's committed impeachable offenses.

"I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War," Hill said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan ."

For months, Republicans have been eyeing the possibility of a third reconciliation bill, which would allow them to approve GOP priorities like additional defense funding without the help of Democrats. But as the House has pushed forward with the effort, it's faced headwinds in the Senate. And now, time is running out.

The upper chamber returns this week to a busy schedule, with intense pressure for Republicans to confirm as many of President Trump's administration and judicial nominees as possible as Democrats are poised to block the GOP's ability to move the president's nominees in the final two years of his term. The Senate is also expected to move forward upon its return on a long-sought permitting reform bill, after a bipartisan deal was reached earlier this fall.

But the push for a party-line bill has continued. Last week, Hegseth urged congressional Republicans to approve additional funds for the Pentagon, saying, "The Department of War must be funded to meet the moment" and calling for a "generational investment" of at least $350 billion.

"We don't back down. And that especially applies now," Hegseth said in a video posted on social media. "Regardless of how people feel about the war — which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon — we need to continue as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military."

Ron Johnson said on "The Takeout" that, as budget chair, he's been "working behind the scenes preparing for reconciliation 3.0.

"If we can gather everybody together, if we get the direction from the White House, exactly what they need — what we can pass through Republican majorities here in the House and the Senate — it's not going to be an easy lift but I'm ready to do it if leadership, if the White House, wants to act."

But the move could also endanger other efforts. If Republicans try to push through another party-line reconciliation package, DeLauro told CBS News that it would threaten bipartisan negotiations on appropriations bills.

Thune told CBS News ahead of the election that he remained open to a third reconciliation bill, but he noted at the time that the votes weren't there.

"It's an option, but it takes 50 votes, which right now we don't have, and maybe that changes after the election," Thune said in late October. "There are some things obviously that the president wants to get done. He wants to deal with the debt limit, defense funding, and we'll see what the appetite is among Democrats to do some of those things, and if we need to do another Republicans-only bill, obviously I'm open to doing that."

articles.title: Fourth Justice Department official resigns following midterms
articles.summary: Another DOJ official has resigned following Democrats' rout in the midterms, which saw Republicans lose their majorities in the House and Senate.
articles.body:
Another Justice Department official has resigned following Democrats' rout in the midterms , which saw Republicans lose their majorities in both the House and Senate.

This time, Brett Shumate, an assistant attorney general who has led the DOJ's Civil Division since June 2025, is the one to go. The Civil Division's responsibilities include defending various federal government policies and representing the government in immigration cases.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a social media post that he accepted Shumate's resignation Nov. 9, and he praised Shumate's efforts challenging local jurisdictions' refusal to work with federal immigration enforcement officials.

Shumate's division "also secured historic settlements to end illegal corporate DEI practices and shuttered dozens of clinics which were providing so-called 'gender affirming care' to minors," Blanche added in his post.

Huge banner of Trump unveiled on Justice Department HQ

Asked why Shumate resigned and whether Blanche was unhappy with any of Shumate's work, the Justice Department referred USA TODAY back to Blanche's social media post praising him.

Last week, Blanche announced the resignation of three other high-level officials: DOJ Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon , U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones and DOJ's National Security Division head John Eisenberg.

The DOJ shakeup comes as Democrats prepare to take control of congressional committees that have the power to issue subpoenas and call officials for testimony as part of congressional oversight. Those committees could look more closely at the Justice Department's activity, which has included several investigations Democrats have decried as politically motivated .

"LAWYER UP," Rep. Robert Garcia, D-California, who is currently the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted on social media Nov. 3, after midterm election results began coming in.
