articles.title: Former GOP governor heads to Capitol Hill before election count is complete: 'Already at work'
articles.summary: Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage heads to Washington as Maine's ranked choice voting process plays out after he topped his rival by 5,000 votes.
articles.body: Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage of Maine is in Washington this week after declaring victory in his congressional race, even as the state’s ranked-choice count continues. LePage narrowly edged out Democratic rival Matt Dunlap, and last week declared victory in the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District. Dunlap conceded on Thursday, Nov. 5. The mostly rural seat is the largest congressional district east of the Mississippi River by area and was won by President Donald Trump in all three of his presidential elections. The apparent victory by LePage would be the only flip from blue to red by House Republicans in a non-redistricted seat in the midterm elections. And it would be rare good news for the GOP after getting trampled by a blue wave that saw Democrats storm back to grab a large House majority as well as recapture the Senate. HEAD HERE FOR THE LATEST RESULTS FROM THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Even though Dunlap conceded to LePage last week, a ranked-choice count kicked off Monday morning. That's because while LePage topped Dunlap by more than 5,000 votes, he fell short of grabbing a majority, which would have prevented ranked-choice voting. According to the Maine Secretary of State, LePage received 49.894% of the total votes cast in the 2nd District race. LePage was in the nation's capital as ranked choice voting got underway. "Paul is already at work in Washington D.C. while the perfunctory process plays out back home. Just like our opponent, who conceded, we are confident in the outcome," longtime LePage campaign strategist Brent Littlefield told Fox News Digital. MAGA VOTERS WEIGH IN ON WHO THEY'D LIKE IN 2028 The former governor is expected to take part Tuesday in a scheduled vote by returning GOP congressional lawmakers and newly elected House Republicans to choose the next minority leader in the race between current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chair Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio. Outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson decided against a bid to lead the House Republicans following the GOP's crushing ballot-box setback. Asked how he succeeded when so many Republicans went down to defeat last week, LePage pointed to "my brand." "I've been governor twice. I've won this district now for the fourth time... My brand. People know me and people trust me and know what I'll say, I'll do," LePage said in a Fox News Digital interview last Wednesday in Bangor, Maine, after declaring victory. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Looking ahead, LePage said, "Hopefully there's still some commonsense in the Democratic Party down there and I hope that I can work with them." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But pointing to far-left Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), LePage argued, "I think we have to rid ourselves of DSA Democrats." And he said Republicans and non-DSA Democrats "have to work together because DSA is a poison for this country."

articles.title: Trump Casts Doubt on Midterm Election Results
articles.summary: The President is following a familiar playbook by sowing doubt about election outcomes after a wave of Republican losses.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump questioned the integrity of the midterm elections on Monday, less than a week after the Republican Party suffered historic defeats in both swing states and former GOP strongholds .

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump asked in a Truth Social post early Monday. "How could the Polls be so wrong???"

"Some early voting 'dumps' were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote," he continued, adding: "It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!" His post did not elaborate on what was meant by the statement.

Trump's unsubstantiated fraud claims come nearly two weeks after he told reporters on Oct. 27 that he would respect the election results "if they're honest elections."

As results came in throughout Nov. 3 and into Nov. 4, Trump seemed to accept the outcome.

"My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," Trump told CBS News in an election-night phone call.

It was a sentiment he repeated in an interview that aired Sunday on 60 Minutes , when he said he would be willing to work with Democrats on immigration, addressing an issue that had been top-of-mind for voters ahead of Election Day. "I think that's something that's actually doable," he said.

By Monday morning, however, Trump was casting doubt on the results. The comment harkens back to Trump's unsubstantiated claims of election interference and ensuing lawsuits after he lost the presidency to Joe Biden in 2020.

Trump was sowing doubt on the 2020 election before voting began, telling the public that August that "the only way we're going to lose this election is if the election is rigged."

Following his loss, Trump refused to concede to Biden. Instead, he began to spread conspiracy theories about widespread election fraud, without evidence.

On Nov. 7, 2020, shortly before news organizations projected Biden's victory, Trump falsely declared on Twitter that he had "WON THIS ELECTION, BY A LOT!"

Echoing Trump's false claims also became a test of loyalty within the Republican Party, with House Speaker Mike Johnson, Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, and former Georgia Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene among those who espoused the false view.

Trump and his allies filed 62 lawsuits challenging or seeking to overturn the results between Nov. 4, 2020, and Jan. 6, 2021, according to the House Jan. 6 committee . Only one produced a victory—a narrow Pennsylvania ruling that didn't establish fraud or change the outcome. Some cases were dismissed on procedural grounds; others failed on the merits.

The legal defeats did not stop Trump from repeating his false claims.

On Dec. 22, 2020, he alleged on social media that Democrats had "DUMPED HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF BALLOTS IN THE SWING STATES LATE IN THE EVENING."

The claims escalated on Jan. 5, 2021, when Trump tweeted : "Washington is being inundated with people who don't want to see an election victory stolen by emboldened Radical Left Democrats."

This followed repeated calls for his supporters to descend upon Washington D.C. and protest the results .

As Congress met to count and certify the Electoral College votes on Jan. 6, 2021, a mob of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol.

His efforts to overturn his 2020 defeat also led to criminal charges. In August 2023, Special Counsel Jack Smith brought four federal charges against Trump, alleging efforts to subvert the results through pressure on officials, fraudulent elector slates, and interference with certification. Trump pleaded not guilty.

On the campaign trail in 2024, he doubled down on his allegations of election interference by urging voters to deliver a victory that was "too big to rig."

The case was dismissed in November that year, after his reelection, because of Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting President.

articles.title: Supreme Court set to pare back federal inmates’ ability to sue officials
articles.summary: The Supreme Court appears likely to bar prison inmates from suing government officials who deny them medical treatment.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday appeared likely to bar federal prison inmates from suing officials who deny them medical treatment in the latest case seeking to roll back the ability to hold federal officials accountable for alleged constitutional violations. The court heard oral arguments over a claim brought by a former federal prison inmate, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges he was denied medical treatment by officers at a Honolulu-based facility in July 2021 after he was beaten by other prisoners during a gang riot. The case focuses on the scope of a 1971 Supreme Court ruling called Bivens v. Six Unknown Fed. Narcotics Agents, which for the first time allowed people to sue federal officials, including prison officials, for civil rights violations. The Trump administration’s recent immigration crackdowns have again put the spotlight on the lack of avenues for accountability for agents who face accusations of violating the Constitution. In Monday’s arguments, the court appeared likely to continue with its recent line of cases that have pared back so-called Bivens claims. Although the court may not overturn the Bivens decision itself, it seems likely to nullify a 1980 Supreme Court ruling that expanded on it, called Carlson v. Green. Then, the justices said federal prison inmates could sue officials for deliberate indifference to their medical needs under the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment, which protects against cruel and unusual punishment. That ruling applies only to federal prison inmates, not those in state prisons who have other ways to bring such claims. In Monday’s argument, several justices in the 6-3 conservative majority pointed out that inmates have other means of seeking redress, including under internal prison procedures and via a federal law called the Federal Tort Claims Act. Under the FTCA, plaintiffs sue the federal government rather than individual officials, and the amount of damages they can win is limited. Conservative Justice Samuel Alito questioned whether Bivens claims provide “anything of value” because most plaintiffs also bring FTCA claims. Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh noted that a “big theme” in the case was that the FTCA provided the necessary remedy for inmates like Watanabe. “If that’s true, that does seem to negate the need” for Bivens claims in the prisons context, he added. The court’s most recent decision rolling back Bivens claims was a 6-3 decision in 2022 that said Border Patrol agents could not be sued. A 2023 NBC News investigation found that the ruling had a major impact on ongoing cases around the country, playing a role in 195 cases being dismissed. The Bivens decision is on such weak ground that the lawyers for the prison worker in Watanabe’s case, nurse Francis Nielsen, asked the justices to overturn it altogether. The Trump administration filed a brief backing the defendant, but did not ask for the Bivens ruling to be overturned. Both Kavanaugh and Chief Justice John Roberts, who were in the majority in the 2022 ruling related to Border Patrol agents, appeared reluctant to overturn Bivens itself in Watanabe’s case. Roberts seemed inclined to give weight to the Justice Department’s arguments, saying it was a “cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question.” Kavanaugh said a dispute over the medical treatment of a prison inmate would be an “odd case” to use as a vehicle to overturn Bivens; the original case involved federal agents involved in a search of a man’s apartment. In the incident at the center of Monday’s case, Watanabe said he asked Nielsen to be treated after complaining about pain following the riot but that the request was denied. Watanabe, who is no longer in federal prison, was later diagnosed with a fractured coccyx and was found to have bone chips embedded in surrounding soft tissue. He then sued, claiming that his Eighth Amendment rights were violated. A federal court rejected Watanabe’s lawsuit, but the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals revived it in a September 2024 ruling. The original Bivens case arose because Congress has never specifically enacted legislation allowing federal officials to face the same kind of civil rights claims that local and state officials regularly deal with. Although legislation has been proposed in Congress, it has yet to gain any momentum.

articles.title: Democrats flip Georgia state House, giving them new control of at least 12 legislative chambers
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of the state House in Georgia after also gaining the governor’s office in last week's midterm election, giving the party control...
articles.body:
Democrats have taken control of the state House in Georgia after also gaining the governor's office in last week's midterm election, giving the party control of each for the first time in more than 20 years.

The flip gives Democrats control of at least 12 new legislative chambers across the U.S. after their major gains at all levels.

It's the biggest gain for either party in a single election since the Republicans took the majority in 20 chambers in 2010 amid the Great Recession and the rise of the conservative tea party movement.

After officials are sworn in later this year and in early 2027, Democrats will have trifectas — control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office — in at least six states where they're currently sharing power with Republicans.

The party running a state government can have a major impact on issues including tax bills, how data center development goes and who qualifies for Medicaid health insurance.

The Associated Press, which has been calling elections since 1848 , on Monday determined the outcome of enough Georgia races to declare Democrats had won the lower chamber.

The news organization has not yet determined who will control the state Senate in North Carolina or either chamber in Alaska.

The Georgia flip breaks up two decades of full GOP control

Republicans have controlled the House in Georgia since 2005 and both the Senate and governor's office since 2003.

Democrats have made gains. In 2020, for instance, Joe Biden narrowly won a plurality in the presidential election there and Democrats prevailed in both U.S. Senate elections. Donald Trump won there in both 2016 and 2024.

This year, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship and Democrats took a House in which Republicans had a comfortable 99-80 majority heading into the election.

As of Monday, Democrats had won 91 House seats and Republicans 86. Three had not been called — including one where the state's secretary of state is investigating the late upload of a memory card containing nearly 400 votes.

While the split government will likely block Democrats from passing some laws, it does open many topics to negotiations.

Races have not been called in 2 states where power is unclear

In North Carolina, Democrats have taken hold of the House and kept the office of governor, where Josh Stein's term has two more years.

As of Monday, the AP hadn't called one race in the Senate. If the GOP holds it, the party would have a 26-24 majority. A Democratic victory would mean a tie, and Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt, a Democrat, would hold the tiebreaking vote.

Both legislative chambers in Alaska currently are controlled by multiparty coalitions. With several races not called, it's unclear how that will shake out for 2027. The AP has also not called the race for governor between Democrat Jonathan Kreiss‑Tomkins and Republican Bernadette Wilson.

The sweeping results give Democrats full power in some states

Currently, there are Republican governors in 26 states and Democratic governors in 24.

Democrats will have at least 28 of those jobs next year, with the race in Kansas also remaining to be called.

Democrats gained control of four more state Senates in Nevada, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, bringing the total they lead to 24. They'll have the majority in at least 27 lower chambers, up from 19, after flips in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Texas and Wisconsin.

Election gains in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin will give Democrats trifectas in all those states.

articles.title: Newly elected Dem's blistering GOP attacks emerge after she courted Republican voters: 'Lit on fire'
articles.summary: South Carolina Democratic Senator-elect Annie Andrews' old posts trashing Republicans and championing transgender rights resurfaced after Election Night.
articles.body: South Carolina’s Democratic senator-elect has a history of trashing Republicans and advocating passionately for transgender rights on social media, with many of those posts reemerging after her victory earlier this month. "The T in LGBTQ+ stands for TRANSGENDER," Annie Andrews, who is set to represent a state President Donald Trump won by roughly 18%, posted in 2023. "If you don’t support trans people, keep your cute pride post in your draft tweets, be better, and try again next year." "Periodic reminder that I support trans kids because I am not an a--hole," she posted around the same time. The posts stand in stark contrast to the more moderate image Andrews presented during her successful campaign against Republican Sen. Darline Graham, when she courted Republicans and independents in the deep-red state and distanced herself from some of her earlier positions on transgender issues. MASSIVE UPSET: ANDREWS DOWNS TRUMP-BACKED GRAHAM IN RUBY-RED SOUTH CAROLINA Beyond transgender issues, where she later distanced herself from certain positions in a campaign ad, Andrews also made her disdain clear for the Republican Party before running for Senate — statements that clashed with the emphasis she placed on bipartisanship while on the campaign trail. In August 2024, Andrews stated that the Republican Party "needs to be lit on fire & thrown in the dumpster & plunged into the deepest depths of the ocean never to be seen again," after some individuals on social media mocked Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz’s son. SC DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS SHE WILL STAND UP TO HER PARTY AS GRAHAM TIES HER TO 'SOCIALIST DEMOCRATS' "Herpes is forever," she said in another post. "JD Vance doesn’t have to be." "Wow they let you out of the kitchen. Congrats," Andrews wrote in a post reacting to GOP Sen. Katie Britt talking about a White House visit, making a jab at Britt with a reference to women being confined to traditional homemaking roles. While Andrews had strong words for Republicans before launching her Senate bid, she worked to appease them in the lead-up to Election Day. At an October town hall billed as "Republicans and Independents for Annie," for instance, she said the campaign was for people more concerned about bills, rural hospitals and government integrity than party labels. She repeatedly stated that she intended to work across the aisle if elected and that her campaign was "not just for Democrats." DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING Andrews made scores of other posts expressing support for abortion access, drag queen story hours and increased restrictions on firearm ownership, among other issues. She reposted one post calling semi-automatic rifles "weapons of war," for instance. "Republicans spent all their money trying to defeat Abdul and hired zero opposition researchers on Annie," independent journalist Zaid Jilani wrote on X, responding to one of Andrews’ pro-transgender resurfaced posts. WHERE TOP DEMOCRAT SENATE CANDIDATES AND THEIR GOP OPPONENTS STAND ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS While some have criticized Republicans for not capitalizing on Andrews’ posts while on the campaign trail, the GOP did dredge old statements in an attempt to dissuade voters from backing her. "Annie Andrews launched her political career fighting for her trans agenda … dozens of comments and tweets advocating for dudes in girls' sports, procedures on minors, and more," National Republican Senatorial Committee advisor Nathan Brand posted in October, responding to an ad released by Andrews disavowing biological men in women’s sports. "Now she is walking it ALL back." Republicans leaned heavily into transgender issues, particularly banning sex change procedures for children and biological men from competing in women’s sports, during the 2026 electoral cycle. While the focus on such issues did not prevent the GOP from losing what are usually safe seats, a number of ballot measures rolling back transgender rights passed in liberal states. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Andrews campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

articles.title: Trump casts doubt on midterm results: ‘How could the polls be so wrong?’
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday asked how the polls could have been “so wrong” after Democrats won back control of both the House and Senate in the midterms, raisi...
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday asked how the polls could have been "so wrong" after Democrats won back control of both the House and Senate in the midterms, raising questions about whether last week's elections were "honest" after signaling he'd accept the results.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???" Trump wrote on TruthSocial.

The president suggested that some early voting dumps were "so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote" and argued that "it's all about the machines" without providing specific evidence.

Days ahead of the election, Trump said he would respect the results if they were "honest."

On Tuesday, Trump told the New York Times that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results of the midterm elections and was prepared to work with Democrats as his party took a shellacking, despite his campaign trail blitz and plea for GOP voters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.

Many polls ahead of the election had forecast a good day for Democrats amid poor approval ratings for Trump and Republicans on the economy, immigration and the war in Iran, though some experts cautioned that a sweep wasn't set in stone.

Ultimately, Democrats won more Senate and House seats than had been expected, and also notched key wins in governor's races across the country -- marking a massive blue wave seen by many as a rebuke against the Trump White House.

Some key races, including the Senate fights in Mississippi and Alaska, were still being counted as of Monday, but Democrats were projected to win significant majorities in both chambers on Capitol Hill.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and other Republicans said ahead of the election that polls showing big leads for Democrats were underestimating Republicans . After Tuesday's results, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) ribbed Johnson that "the polls were wrong" in that they underestimated Democrats.

"Donald Trump's pathetic return to election denialism was inevitable," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a post on X, responding to the president's latest election comments.

"He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure," Schumer said.

Conservative pundit Megyn Kelly, who said last week that the GOP needs to "learn how to win without daddy on the ballot, shared Trump's post with the comment: "just stop."

Trump has continued to raise unsubstantiated claims of widespread fraud during the 2020 election, when he lost his reelection bid to former President Biden — which has frustrated some in his own party who want to move on. His refusal to commit to a peaceful transfer of power led up to the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.

articles.title: Slotkin lawyer warns Blanche not to obey Trump’s ‘frivolous’ demand to investigate her
articles.summary: Donald Trump told the DOJ to investigate Elissa Slotkin. Her lawyer is lawyer warns Todd Blanche not to obey.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — An attorney for Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin is warning Attorney General Todd Blanche not to bow to President Donald Trump’s demand for a criminal investigation into her political speech. Over the weekend, Trump posted on his social media platform that he was demanding the Justice Department look into the Michigan senator’s recent comments about how Democratic investigations into the Trump administration could send a “deterrence message” to young people thinking about joining the administration in its final two years. “By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!” Trump wrote. In a letter to Blanche made public Monday, Preet Bharara, the former U.S. attorney in the Southern District of New York, wrote that it “should not be hard to make clear that we do not live in an authoritarian regime where mere criticism of the powerful can land anyone in legal peril and possibly prison.” “That requires a clear and public statement confirming that the Department will not pursue this investigation against Senator Slotkin,” he wrote. The Justice Department didn’t comment on Trump’s post. But in a statement Monday, a Justice Department spokesperson declined to rule out an investigation. “Sen. Slotkin said publicly that the prospect of future investigations should deter young people from joining this administration,”the spokesperson said. “The Department believes public service should not be met with threats of retribution, and this Department is committed to ending the weaponization of government. We follow the facts and the law.” The attorney general is appointed by the president and is a member of his Cabinet, but it’s still highly unusual for the White House to publicly demand an investigation. The Justice Department has long sought to separate politics from the law. But under Blanche, Trump’s former personal attorney, the department has investigated many of the president’s perceived political enemies. Slotkin, a former CIA and Defense Department official, was also one of a group of lawmakers the Trump administration tried and failed to indict earlier this year over a social media video. A few weeks before the midterm elections, where the GOP saw massive losses, she spoke at the University of Chicago, arguing that Democrats should focus investigative efforts on those who enable Trump. She said she hoped to deter young people coming out of school from joining the administration. “I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that,’” Slotkin said. “I want that deterrence message sent.” In his post on Truth Social over the weekend, Trump accused Slotkin of “going to go after all young people that believe in Republican Values, and that give even the slightest inclination to be a Republican.” Trump’s demand came weeks after Trump ally Mike Davis requested that Harmeet Dhillon — who has since resigned as head of the Civil Rights Division — launch an investigation of Slotkin. Bharara wrote that Slotkin’s comments were “entirely lawful” and protected by the First Amendment as well as the “speech and debate” clause of the Constitution, which protects members of Congress. “There is no conceivable basis to investigate the Senator for reminding members of the executive branch who aid the President’s law breaking that there will be accountability for their actions, or expressing the hope that Americans decline to serve in an administration where leaders may ask them to violate the law or misuse taxpayer dollars,” Bharara wrote. “Indeed, the Senator’s statement reinforces the rule of law.” Bharara asked Blanche to publicly decline to follow Trump’s command. “The Department should stop threatening our constitutional freedoms and make clear that you will not again launch another frivolous investigation at the taxpayers’ expense,” he wrote. Bharara’s letter noted that it had been less than a year since the administration failed to indict Slotkin and five other members of Congress over a social media video that reminded members of the military and intelligence communities of their duties not to follow unlawful orders. “Thankfully, the anonymous citizens of a Washington D.C. grand jury unanimously rejected the Department’s attempt to punish a perceived political adversary for her lawful — indeed, constitutionally privileged — speech,” Bharara wrote.

articles.title: Republican Thomas Massie will force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
articles.body:
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, given Republicans will remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says he wants to push President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth, who will hold a news conference on Tuesday about Massie's move, said he was not concerned.

Massie formally introduced the articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon.

"We're not worried about that," Hegseth said when asked by reporters about the impending resolution earlier on Monday, adding he would hold a news conference Tuesday morning "on that very topic".

Hegseth's last news conference was in May.

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He is known across the country for also pushing the administration to release federal files on the deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and is now pressing for a vote in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said his push to rid the administration of Hegseth is meant to prevent a Democrat spectacle next year.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."

"President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," he also said.

Impeaching a cabinet secretary is very rare. The impeachment must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. As with presidential impeachments, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.

The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not agree on either one.

Now Massie has introduced his resolution, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson must schedule a time to consider it within two days. Along with voting on the resolution directly, the House has the options to vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

Massie will likely have the support of the Democrats in the House, with that party's leader, Hakeem Jeffries, saying on Sunday that he is a "hard yes" on impeachment. But Massie would still need to win over members of his own party.

Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that the impeachment measure is "likely to pass the House because the Republican majority is so slim".

"And there are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he added.

Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.

Loge also says the chances that Hegseth will survive until the end of Trump's term are "pretty slim", and he thinks it's more likely that the president will remove the secretary than lawmakers will vote to impeach him.

The Senate requires a two-thirds vote to convict, a high threshold that would be hard to meet in the current congressional term. When the Democrats take over in January, they still will not have enough seats to convict Hegseth without Republican support – even if Alaska and Mississippi end up with Democratic senators once all ballots are counted.

The House has passed a War Powers resolution - a measure seeking to halt Trump from taking further military action in Iran - multiple times this year, with Massie's support. The Senate also passed a War Powers resolution over the summer.

But Massie's disagreement with Hegseth goes beyond Iran, he said in the statement.

He accused Hegseth of intimidating critics of the Trump administration, kidnapping foreign leaders and ignoring congressional war powers resolutions.

Loge suspects the negative attention Hegseth has attracted might be what prompts Trump to fire him, saying the secretary "has been pushing the limits of decency and legality for a long time".

"Secretary Hegseth is a big personality, and I'm not sure I'd want to be a big personality that's drawing attention from President Trump these days," Loge said. "That's not a way to guarantee job security."

articles.title: Democratic lawmakers seek to restore deportation protections to Afghans in the U.S.
articles.summary: A pair of House Democrats will try to bypass Republican leaders and force a vote to restore Temporary Protected Status to Afghan nationals in the United States by introducing a discharge petition when Congress returns Monday night.
articles.body: A pair of House Democrats will try to bypass Republican leaders and force a vote to restore Temporary Protected Status to Afghan nationals in the United States by introducing a discharge petition when Congress returns Monday night. Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., and Rep. Sam Liccardo, D-Calif., will file the petition, which would require signatures from 218 members to bring forth legislation to grant Afghans protection from deportation until mid-2029. TPS, created by Congress in 1990, is a Department of Homeland Security program that allows migrants to live and work in the U.S. for up to 18 months if their home countries have been designated as unsafe. The time period can be extended. President Donald Trump’s administration terminated the status for Afghanistan in May 2025, a designation that former President Joe Biden’s administration had granted in 2022. “This administration is returning TPS to its original temporary intent,” then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said at the time. She added that “Afghanistan has had an improved security situation, and its stabilizing economy no longer prevent them from returning to their home country.” While the Trump administration recently planned to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan, a federal judge last week temporarily blocked that move. Crow and Liccardo would need all current House Democrats and a handful of Republicans to sign on to their discharge petition to reach the necessary 218 signatures. The pair already introduced a special rule on Oct. 1, allowing them to start collecting signatures as soon as they submit the petition on Monday. “Our Afghan partners put their lives on the line to help protect American servicemembers like me,” Crow, who served as a paratrooper and an Army Ranger in Iraq and Afghanistan, said in a statement. “I’m working to force a vote that will protect Afghans already in the United States because I won’t let our nation leave these brave Afghans behind.” If Crow and Liccardo are successful in reaching the 218-signature threshold, GOP leaders would be forced to bring forward the Afghanistan TPS Act for a floor vote. That bill, which the pair introduced in July, would grant TPS to Afghans until July 2029. The legislation would need a majority vote on the House floor to pass. The bill already has four Republican co-sponsors: Reps. Don Bacon of Nebraska, Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, Joe Wilson of South Carolina, and Morgan Luttrell of Texas. It also has the backing of Rep. Kevin Kiley, a Republican-turned-independent from California. “Thousands of Afghans risked their lives alongside American troops because our country made them a promise: We would not abandon them,” Liccardo said. “Now, we risk sending them back into the hands of the very Taliban forces they helped us fight. This cannot wait until the Democratic majority takes over.” The bill has the backing of more than 50 organizations, including Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, Veterans of Foreign Wars and Amnesty International USA. Once rare, discharge petitions have been successful several times in the 119th Congress as a small number of Republicans have bucked party leadership to join Democrats in getting measures to the floor. In April, the House voted to reinstate temporary protection for Haitian immigrants after a few Republicans joined with Democrats on that discharge petition. The legislation passed 224-204, with 10 Republicans joining all Democrats in support. While the White House had vowed that Trump would veto the bill, Senate Republicans blocked the legislation from going to his desk. Other successful discharge petitions have included votes on aid to Ukraine, extending Affordable Care Act subsidies and the Epstein Files Transparency Act put forth by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif. The House is scheduled to be in town this week and next before a Thanksgiving recess.

articles.title: Two security breaches near White House prompt brief lockdown
articles.summary: Active investigations are under way after a vehicle crashed at Lafayette Park and a second individual jumped a barrier.
articles.body:
Two people have been detained near the White House following a pair of security breaches, according to the United States Secret Service agency (USSS).

One of the incidents, which occurred Monday morning, involved a suspect who drove a vehicle onto the pavement at Lafayette Park, which sits directly in front of the White House.

Secret Service Police and National Guard units responded to reports of the vehicle crash at about 10am local time (15:00 GMT), according to a spokesperson for the federal law enforcement agency.

They converged on the northern edge of Lafayette Park near 16th and H Streets Northwest.

Around the same time, another suspect jumped a security barrier in the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. It is not clear if the two events were related.

President Donald Trump was inside the executive residence when the incidents occurred, prompting a brief White House lockdown and the closure of the surrounding roads.

The lockdown was lifted an hour later, according to the White House press pool.

Video footage of the incident captured a silver sedan emitting blankets of smoke as law enforcement officers surrounded it. It shows the driver exiting the vehicle and swinging at the gathered officers.

“The driver was combative with law enforcement, but was quickly placed under arrest,” the Secret Service statement read.

The Metropolitan Police Department’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit was called in to conduct a vehicle sweep after the driver was taken into custody.

Around the same time as police were dealing with the combative driver, “a second individual jumped a barricade near the northwest corner of Lafayette Park”, according to USSS.

Authorities have not stated what charges the two people arrested may be facing. Both incidents remain under investigation.

articles.title: Gaza-born Democratic Socialist launches primary bid against Sen John Fetterman
articles.summary: Democratic Socialists of America member Ahmed Moor launched a Pennsylvania primary challenge against Sen. John Fetterman over Israel support.
articles.body: A Gaza-born member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has launched a primary challenge against Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., setting up a race against one of the Senate's most vocal supporters of Israel. In a post on X, Palestinian-American writer and businessman Ahmed Moor, 42, announced his campaign to unseat Fetterman in Pennsylvania's Democratic primary. "I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing," Moor wrote. "I’m calling for accountability for genocide, for ICE and for corruption. And finally, for the protection of our civil liberties in America." DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT Moor is part of a broader wave of DSA members seeking public office amid growing progressive dissatisfaction with moderate Democrats. Fetterman has drawn ire from his party's left wing for his staunch support of Israel in its war against Hamas, as well as his willingness to align with President Donald Trump on select policy issues. FETTERMAN TROLLS THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA AS ISRAEL KILLS HAMAS TERRORISTS: 'CRY HARDER' According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, Moor moved to Pennsylvania as a child, earned degrees from the University of Pennsylvania and Harvard University, and worked in finance before embarking on a career in journalism. Prior to launching his campaign, he lived in Jordan before returning to Philadelphia with his wife to raise their children. On his campaign website, Moor sharply criticized U.S. foreign aid to Israel. "A few years ago my birthplace was turned to rubble in a genocide funded by our tax dollars, with the support of politicians on both sides of the aisle who can't find money for transit or removing asbestos from our schools," the website states. articles.title: Schumer's grip on power slips as Dems begin to revolt against him, eye new leadership
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer says he expects no challenge for Senate Democratic leader, but newcomers and Chris Van Hollen are reportedly mulling alternatives.
articles.body: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is riding high after flipping the Senate, but a growing rebellion among longtime and fresh-faced Senate Democrats may throw a wrench in his plan to seek another term as the top dog in the upper chamber. The top Democrat, who has led the Senate Democratic caucus for nearly a decade, has made clear he intends to run for another term as leader and take on the role of majority leader once more. Schumer only needs a majority of Senate Democrats to vote for him to keep the job, but some want to take stock before jumping in to back him. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' "We need a conversation about leadership going forward, because we need new energy and ideas," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters on Tuesday when asked whether he supported Schumer. But he quickly followed up by noting that he expected that Schumer would be "re-elected as leader, because no one has come forth willing to take the position. But we need a conversation about leadership." Schumer, during an appearance on the New York Times’ "The Daily" podcast, was asked if he expected a challenge in running for another term as leader. "No," he said. THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL When pressed, Schumer argued that the Senate Democratic caucus is "focused on moving forward." "Everyone’s very happy with what we all did. But this is just the beginning," Schumer said. "As I said before, and I’ll say it again and again to my caucus, to the country, to everybody: If we don’t deliver, all this will go away. This is just the first step. But I think we’re united together to do that." Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer’s office for comment on unrest among Democrats over his plan to seek another term. Many of the newcomers to the Senate, which spans the ideological gamut from moderate to progressive, have made clear they won’t support Schumer, including the likes of Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton and Troy Jackson. JOE MANCHIN WARNS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE GAINING GROUND AS DEMOCRATS REMAIN SILENT And the sentiment that the immediate future of Democratic leadership needs to be litigated is percolating among some Senate Democrats, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is favored by progressives in the upper chamber to run for the job. "I’ve said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic caucus," Van Hollen said during an appearance at Crooked Con over the weekend. "We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers," he continued. "And that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we’re going to go." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And Van Hollen, who has previously said his focus was more on "kicking the tires" on a run for higher office in 2028, is reportedly mulling a bid for Schumer’s job, according to Politico. articles.title: Hegseth impeachment vote looms as House Republicans privately warn it could pass
articles.summary: Several House Republicans believe Pete Hegseth's impeachment could pass as Rep. Thomas Massie forces a privileged resolution vote this week.
articles.body: The House of Representatives is barreling toward a vote on impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth this week, and several GOP lawmakers think it could very well pass. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., is triggering a vote on impeaching Hegseth by introducing a privileged resolution on Monday, a mechanism for forcing consideration of bills that House majority leaders otherwise would have ignored. A privileged resolution must be considered within two legislative days, putting the vote on Wednesday at the latest. Massie read his resolution on the House floor on Monday, as is custom, which took over an hour. It comes as fallout from the war in Iran, including high gas prices, is blamed as a key factor in Republicans' significant losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. HEGSETH FACES BIPARTISAN IMPEACHMENT THREAT AFTER IRAN WAR GETS BLAME FOR GOP MIDTERM SLAUGHTER Massie told Fox News Digital last week that he would trigger the vote when Congress returned after the midterms if Hegseth did not first resign. Hegseth, for his part, called the impeachment effort against him a "shame" that "won't work" in a video posted to X on Friday. HEGSETH DEMANDS $350B FOR MILITARY, FIRES BACK AT DEM IMPEACHMENT PUSH But several House Republicans told Fox News Digital on Thursday that they believed Hegseth could very well be impeached. Sources said a combination of absences of Republican members who lost their elections and negative sentiment toward Hegseth's conduct could be enough to tip it over the edge. The majority of Republicans are still expected to oppose the move, however. Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, a critic of the war, said he was not in favor of impeaching Hegseth. I think it's an effort to scapegoat Pete Hegseth for Congress shirking their own duty and, frankly, the president taking action that, in my view, is unconstitutional — but it's also not unprecedented," Davidson told Fox News Digital. "What would be unprecedented is to hold the Secretary of Defense accountable for a decision the president makes. Or frankly, it would have been unprecedented for the Secretary of Defense to kind of break ranks on something that is clearly not unprecedented in terms of what has become the standard operating procedure for administrations going back to the Korean War." Massie's impeachment resolution includes eight articles having to do with the war in Iran, striking suspected drug boats in the Caribbean, U.S. strikes against Yemen, and the extradition of now-former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH Notably, another impeachment article accuses Hegseth of suppressing free speech by retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., over a video in which Kelly urged troops to resist "unlawful orders." A privileged resolution notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it. The last Cabinet secretary to be impeached was Biden administration Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, whom Republicans accused of a dereliction of duty at the U.S.-Mexico border. It was quickly scuttled without a trial in the last Democrat-controlled Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It's not immediately clear how House GOP leaders plan to deal with Massie's resolution.

articles.title: White House doubles down after Trump angers base by floating illegal alien deal with Dems
articles.summary: Trump signaled willingness to work a deal for illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for over a decade, drawing fierce amnesty backlash.
articles.body: The White House on Monday morning wouldn't rule out the administration working with Democrats on a "deal" for illegal immigrants who have been living in the U.S. for more than a decade as Republicans prepare to lose control of Congress in January. President Donald Trump, in his first sit-down interview since sweeping GOP midterm losses, opened the door to the possibility of considering amnesty. "The President never said the word amnesty," a White House official insisted to Fox News Digital. "We want Democrats to show their cards," the official revealed. TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS They said, "There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump." "Thanks to his efforts more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. and we have the most secure border in American history. Like the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to improve the lives of Americans and Make America Safe Again." In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday, host Ross Douthat asked Trump how he is open to working with Democrats on immigration as he enters a lame-duck final stretch of his presidency. "I'd love to do something on immigration," the president replied. "I think [immigration] both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law — that was that they came into the country illegally." Trump, however, maintained that there are people in the United States who want to see all illegal aliens deported. FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE But, Trump said, "if they're good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases paying taxes, and there's a large group of people that think they should be allowed to stay." "When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," he said, adding that people who he called "far-right" want deportations regardless of whether the illegal alien is working. FIRST ON FOX: DEMS' AFFORDABILITY CRUSADE COLLIDES WITH EYE-POPPING PRICE TAG FOR SOCIALIST IMMIGRATION PLANS While Trump didn't say "amnesty," as the White House noted, he signaled in the interview his willingness to "work a deal" for people who have been in the United States illegally for "10 and 15 years" who haven't committed other crimes. Rep. Maria Salazar, R-Fla., a longtime proponent of giving legal status to illegal aliens, celebrated Trump's comments on X. "Well done, Mr. President! What you described on 60 Minutes is what the Dignity Act is all about," she said in the post. Salazar's Dignity Act would offer legal status to people who have been in the United States continuously since 2020, provided they haven't committed other crimes and pay a restitution fee and back taxes. The White House wouldn't clarify what such a deal could entail when asked Monday. Notably, the interview was taped before Stephen Miller, a notorious immigration hawk, was selected to be Trump's new chief of staff. Immigration restrictionism has been Trump's calling card since he first ran for president beginning in 2015. His comments in the interview that aired Sunday drew a sharp reaction from those favor immigration restriction. TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES "To be clear, if President Trump struck an amnesty deal with the Democrat-controlled Congress, it would be a bigger betrayal than starting the foolish war in Iran," commentator Steve Cortes said on X, adding a clip of Trump promising "the largest deportation operation in the history of our country" during a campaign rally in 2024. "This plan absolutely guarantees that Texas never again votes Republican," said radio show host Anthony Cumia. "More states will turn permanently blue if illegals are given amnesty. Regan did the same this and California became a forever democrat state. Trump can do the same to Texas. Disgusting." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Someone needs to tell Trump: Any amnesty deal with Democrats will destroy the Republican Party," said X personality Kelly McCarty. "We voted for NO amnesty and mass deportations of ALL illegals. No compromises. No exceptions."

articles.title: Trump open to talking to Democrats on immigration after midterms, but Mullin stresses no amnesty
articles.summary: (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that he and President Donald Trump haven’t yet discussed any concrete immigration policy chan...
articles.body:
FOREST HEIGHTS, Md. (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that he and President Donald Trump haven't yet discussed any concrete immigration policy changes in the aftermath of the midterm elections as the president shifts his tone on deportations and says he's open to working with Democrats on the issue .

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a conference near Washington, D.C., Mullin also said he is strongly opposed to any amnesty for people living in the U.S. illegally — long a red line for Republicans that has contributed to the intractableness of the immigration issue.

The midterms highlighted voters' disaffection toward the administration's hard-line immigration enforcement activities and Trump has since said not only that he could work with Democrats on immigration but also, during an interview with "60 Minutes" Sunday, said that his deportation policy was too aggressive for voters.

Mullin on Monday reiterated Trump's willingness to work with Democrats on the issue.

Mullin, who was a senator and house representative before becoming Trump's Homeland Security secretary earlier this year, said after the election he's been fielding calls from Democrats that he worked with in Congress on bipartisan issues.

"I've let the president know that those calls are coming in. And the president has said, you know, let's start working with them and then let's meet at some point. So that's the extent of the conversation," Mullin said in a briefing with reporters. "We haven't had any conversation just on policy."

Trump since the election has elevated Stephen Miller , the key architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions about how cooperation with Democrats might look so long as enforcement remains strict. Mullin called him in a post on social media last week an "excellent choice."

Mullin, who said he worked with Democrats while he was in Congress including on immigration reform, said he thought a bipartisan approach was the only way to get anything done. But the secretary also pushed back decisively against any type of agreement that would include amnesty for people living illegally in the U.S.

"I was working on immigration reform when I was in the House and when I was in the Senate. I think the only way you can actually get it is by a bipartisan approach. But amnesty's never going to be a solution. We're never gonna allow amnesty to happen. So that's a full stop," said Mullin.

The Homeland Security secretary raised the issue of DACA — a form of protection from deportation for children brought to the country illegally by their parents. He said figuring out a way to legalize their status would be up to Congress.

"Now, if we wanna have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that'll be up to Congress to do that," Mullin said.

Mullin spoke on the sidelines of a conference about drones and counter-drone technologies in the Washington, D.C., suburbs.

articles.title: Articles of impeachment against Hegseth introduced in the House as GOP criticism over the Iran war mounts after midterm rout
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican from Kentucky, introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as Congress ret...
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican from Kentucky, introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as Congress returned to Washington, D.C., to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates. Read the original story below.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran following the historic drubbing Republicans took from Democrats in this week's midterm elections. But President Trump has said he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet.

"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters. On Thursday, Trump said Hegseth had "done a fantastic job," Reuters reported .

The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor this week.

"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat.

According to CBS News , though, Trump "has been asking advisers" whether Hegseth should stay or go. The White House has denied reports that Hegseth would leave his job in a post-election shake-up, the BBC reported . The Pentagon has said Hegseth is "100 percent committed" to serving through the end of Trump's term.

Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices.

Hegseth has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing U.S. officials. Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict, the Journal reported.

Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war."

The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning."

"He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress."

Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him.

"I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it."

Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Friday that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer told NewsNation .

When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list.

"In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month .

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky and vocal Trump critic, said he intends to force a House vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as next week, citing violations of the War Powers Resolution, bypassing Congress on war declarations and unlawful military actions in several countries.

Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the Republican primary — introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote.

In a post on X Wednesday , Massie wrote that "there is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns."

In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Thursday afternoon, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me."

Tillis responded on X. "Cabinet secretaries shouldn't be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos," he wrote, adding that the issue was "the incompetence you've displayed" and "the bad advice you've given to president."

articles.title: Supreme Court allows Big Bend border wall plans in win for Trump
articles.summary: Texans in the Big Bend area say a border wall threatens their land, lives and livelihoods. The Trump administration has fast-tracked construction.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court said the Trump administration can move ahead for now on plans to build a border wall in a remote swath of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.

The court on Nov. 9 paused a judge's order that halted controversial construction of roads and barriers across the Big Bend region while a challenge brought by a riverboat guide, environmentalists and a group formed to preserve a church is being litigated.

Opponents say the construction will result in the permanent alteration of "one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States."

In an unsigned opinion, the court said that Congress has expressed a "clear preference for expeditious border construction," which outweighs "any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm."

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the court's three liberals, was the only justice to publicly dissent.

Go inside Big Bend as border wall resistance lines the Rio Grande

President Donald Trump campaigned on tough immigration enforcement and border controls, and he has made expansion of the border wall a key campaign promise.

The administration has fast-tracked construction, waiving dozens of environmental regulations.

The administration argues that Congress gave the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security the ability to bypass legal requirements if they are slowing construction of border barriers.

"Congress was hardly shy about the major powers it granted the Secretary," the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in the administration's emergency appeal .

A federal judge in Texas ruled last month that the law limits waivers of regulations to "areas of high illegal entry."

The Big Bend region spans 517 miles – more than a quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border – but the rugged area has the lowest number of apprehensions of any Southwest border sector, according to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone.

The Justice Department said Cardone lacked authority to intervene because the waivers can only be challenged if they violated the Constitution and the dispute is over how to interpret a statute.

Cardone said the dispute raises the larger constitutional question of whether it would be a violation of the separation of powers for Congress to have given the administration as much authority as it says it has.

But the Supreme Court said the administration was "exceedingly likely" to win its argument that there is no constitutional dispute.

The judge also said a temporary halt was needed while the legal battle continues because construction could result in the permanent loss of protected wilderness that benefits tourism, recreation, farming, ranching, spirituality, aesthetic sensibilities and education.

In August, the administration paused construction after local residents staged a protest.

While federal officials did not plan to build a wall through Big Bend National Park, public lands advocates were outraged when contractors began bulldozing access roads through the area in early to mid-August. Videos recorded by activists captured bulldozers and track hoes cutting through the desert soil and across cliffs.

Texans in the Big Bend area, including some Republicans, say a border wall in the region threatens their land, lives and livelihoods. Any physical barrier could jeopardize the landscape that draws more than half a million visitors annually and drives the local economy.

Local landowner Luis Armendariz Spencer, who owns property along the river, says the region does not need a border wall, arguing that the remote terrain and mountains have long deterred illegal crossings. articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Senate advances permitting bill, teeing up passage The Senate voted Monday to advance a major bipartisan bill that aims to speed up the construction of energy and other infrastructure projects — clearing a key hurdle toward the measure becoming law. © Greg Nash…
articles.body:
Senate advances permitting bill, teeing up passage

The Senate voted Monday to advance a major bipartisan bill that aims to speed up the construction of energy and other infrastructure projects — clearing a key hurdle toward the measure becoming law.

The vote was 73-25, teeing up likely Senate passage in the weeks ahead.

The bill in question, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, seeks to make it easier to build — at the expense of some of the nation’s environmental laws . It will make it harder for opponents to sue to block projects on environmental grounds and also hamper the ability of states and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to preemptively block them, which has historically held up ventures such as fossil fuels and mining.

However, Democrats argued Monday that the legislation will be good for both the climate and consumers’ wallets.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) told reporters ahead of the vote that the legislation is expected to save consumers about $60 to $80 each month.

He also said it will prevent between 1.5 and 1.8 gigatons of greenhouse gas emissions.

Whitehouse said it will increase the nation’s wind capacity by 25 percent, solar capacity by 28 percent and battery storage capacity by 70 percent.

Welcome to The Hill’s Energy & Environment newsletter, I’m Rachel Frazin — keeping you up to speed on the policies impacting everything from oil and gas to new supply chains.

Did someone forward you this newsletter? Subscribe here.

How policy will affect the energy and environment sectors now and in the future:

President Trump on Monday said he would not approve new wind turbines despite his support for a permitting reform bill that seeks to ease the passage of all forms of energy, including wind.

The Supreme Court is allowing border barrier construction to continue in and around Big Bend National Park in Texas, in a win for the Trump administration.

Former President Jimmy Carter’s family farm in Georgia has been sold to a conservation group for $8.5 million, with plans to preserve the land and eventually open it to the public.

articles.title: Cornyn declines to say if he voted for Paxton, cites Paxton’s ‘corruption’ as issue
articles.summary: Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) declined to say Monday whether he voted for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate in Texas’s Senate race who defeated Cornyn earlier this year in a primary runoff election, and cited Paxton’s “corruption” as a major reason why he lost to Democrat James Talarico. “The Republican Party treated…
articles.body:
Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) declined to say Monday whether he voted for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate in Texas’s Senate race who defeated Cornyn earlier this year in a primary runoff election, and cited Paxton’s “corruption” as a major reason why he lost to Democrat James Talarico.

“The Republican Party treated corruption, particularly in the person of Paxton, as just a normal thing. And I think that was vehemently rejected” by voters, Cornyn said.

“Corruption was an issue, not only at the local level or the state level, but also at the national level, too. And I think that contributed to the landslide that swept almost everybody in the process,” he added.

Asked if he voted for Paxton, Cornyn replied: “My vote is a private matter.”

Cornyn argued that the Democratic victory in the Texas Senate race is not a sign that Texas has “turned blue” or become more aligned with the Democratic Party on policy issues.

Instead, he argued that the results in the Lone Star State were largely driven by voters favoring Talarico as a candidate over Paxton.

“Texas did not turn blue. It was really a referendum on their choices in the Senate race and the president’s poor approval rating. I don’t think ideologically or philosophically the state has shifted,” he said.

Cornyn met with Talarico on Capitol Hill on Monday and said his successor deserves “a chance” to be successful, calling him a “decent” person.

He said he advised Talarico to resist pressure from Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) to vote frequently along party lines, arguing that would imperil his chances of being reelected.

“We obviously have very different political points of view, but I think he’s basically a decent, honest person. So, I think he’s entitled to a fair chance,” Cornyn said.

“He’s going to be on the ballot in six years in a red state,” he asserted.

Cornyn warned Talarico that he will come under pressure from fellow Democrats to vote in ways that don’t necessarily match a majority of Texans’ views.

“It’s going to be interesting to see how he conducts himself because I told him Schumer is a very relentless and smart and demanding leader, and my guess is he’s going to have to break with the leadership at some critical junctures in the future if he wants to get reelected,” he said.

Cornyn did not endorse Paxton in the general election, though he did pledge to support the GOP ticket in Texas.

articles.title: Returning to Washington, Republicans vent anger, frustrations after midterm drubbing
articles.summary: Republicans returned to Washington on Monday following an election rout that saw them lose both chambers of Congress for the final two years of President Trump’s time in office. Their mood matched their fortunes. The blue wave that crashed into the midterms has forced a reckoning within the GOP, sparking questions about what went wrong,…
articles.body:
Republicans returned to Washington on Monday following an election rout that saw them lose both chambers of Congress for the final two years of President Trump’s time in office.

The blue wave that crashed into the midterms has forced a reckoning within the GOP, sparking questions about what went wrong, who bears the blame and how to right the listing ship in time to salvage the 2028 cycle. Those conversations had started last week, but they’re taking off now that Republicans are back in the Capitol, licking wounds, seeking answers and pointing fingers.

“There’s a lot of pissed off people in there right now,” Rep. Richard McCormick (R-Ga.) said, pointing to the House voting chamber. “A lot of people who are pointing fingers. Some of it rightfully so on where the spend was, how we raise money, what the messaging was, where the message came from. You can see people say all kinds of things.”

Rep. Troy Nehls (R-Texas) argued that he would give Congress an F on its report card.

“It was a horrible election year,” he said. “I mean, I think the American people have a right to be upset with our performance, our performance as Congress as a whole.”

The tone across the Capitol was similarly dour. Some Republicans said the party simply lost touch with voters when it came to policy priorities.

“I just think that you look at what this Congress chose to do, this Congress…made its priorities what were not the people’s priorities, and when you abandon pro-lifers, when you abandon the needy, when you abandon [the] poor, when you abandon working people, the American people might have something to say about that,” said Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.).

“I see a lot of blame shifting going on in all of these postmortems. I think maybe it’s time for people who are in Congress to take responsibility for what Congress did,” Hawley added.

Last week’s midterms stunned political observers of all stripes — lawmakers and outside experts alike — as Republicans lost both the House and Senate by margins that few predicted beforehand. In the House, the wave means Democrats are on track to hold roughly 260 seats next year, while Senate Democrats could control 56 seats. Both numbers were almost unthinkable heading into the polls.

How Republicans ultimately react won’t be known for some time. But in the near term, some Republicans have called for GOP leadership elections to be delayed, arguing that the party needs to self-reflect on their brutal beating last week and make changes internally before moving forward as a conference.

“We are less than a week removed from Tuesday’s elections, and need to understand how and why we lost the trust of the American people,” House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) wrote on X. “We also need, as a Conference, to address how our rules have empowered members to vote against rules, bills, and even the Speaker. Failing to address these issues before choosing someone new to lead our Conference is doing a disservice to whoever we choose as Republican Leader.”

Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-N.J.), whose midterm defeat stunned many observers who deemed him to be safe, pointed to the familiar factors driving his party’s decline: High gas prices, a war in Ukraine that’s dragged on, and a war with Iran of the type that Trump had campaigned against.

“A lot of things went wrong. Some of them you can control, some of them you can’t. … It all queued up at just the right time,” he said. “I hope we do learn. We’ve got to stop arguing with each other [and] get a message.”

Amid the finger pointing, some House Republicans said the blame should fall squarely on the Senate, where the esoteric rules of the chamber prevented GOP leaders from moving dozens of House-passed bills over the past two years.

“I think Mike Johnson, Speaker Johnson, and the House did everything they could. We sent a lot of legislation to the Senate, and there’s over, 500 or 600 bills over there that are just sitting there. America First bills. I have some of them, and the Senate’s done nothing with them,” Nehls said.

Still others pointed fingers at the president, whose immigration crackdown struck a nerve with a majority of Americans and seemed to shift the Hispanic vote over to Democrats.

“There was a lot of people who voted for the president because of border security who didn’t like his overzealous ICE enforcement actions, and he basically admitted the same,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his primary to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton earlier in the year. Paxton then faced a shocking defeat to Democrat James Talarico in the primary.

While Republicans were largely gloomy about their fate on election night, some were also quick to point out the simple reality that, in politics, the pendulum is always swinging back and forth, and fortunes change with a shift in political environments. With that in mind, some were already looking ahead to that cycle when they’ll be back in power.

“This is politics,” Van Drew said. “My wife still loves me; my kids still love me; my grandkids still love me; my German shepherd still loves me. I’m OK.”

Van Drew is already planning to run again in 2028.

articles.body:
President Trump on Monday shot back at efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth,” Trump said in a Truth Social post Monday night.

“With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” the president added in his post.

On Monday, Massie followed through on a promise to bring articles of impeachment targeting Hegseth. The Kentucky Republican read the articles out loud on the House floor a little after 2 p.m. EST.

Earlier in the day, Hegseth said he wasn’t “worried“ about Massie’s effort and said he would have a press conference on the matter the following morning.

Last weekend , Trump expressed concerns about some Democrats pushing for the impeachment of Republican officials. The president called the threats “extortion at the highest level” and requested the Department of Justice “look into this.”

“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people … with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so, and there have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post Saturday.

Trump’s post came after Democrats locked down the House and Senate in this year’s midterms, with the party set to take control of the chambers in January.

The Hill has reached out to Massie’s office for comment.
